KW Delhi 6.what: One of the two KW Group projects Yamini qualifies leads for.
KW Delhi 6.why: Leads arrive tagged D6 or BP, and the n8n router splits on that tag so each project gets its own reply templates and its own broadcast schedule.

Blue Pearl.what: The second KW Group project Yamini handles, alongside Delhi 6.
Blue Pearl.why: Same pipeline, separate templates and broadcasts. The split happens at the router, which is why there are BP and D6 variants of most WhatsApp workflows.

Cratio.what: The CRM the sales floor actually works in, external to this estate.
Cratio.why: It is where a qualified lead has to land for anyone to act on it. The four AI Bot fields on a Cratio lead are the intended destination for Yamini's verdicts, and they have been null since Aug 2025.

n8n.what: A self-hosted workflow automation tool, running in Docker on srv1340120.
n8n.why: Every integration in the estate is an n8n workflow rather than bespoke code, which is why the workflow list is the closest thing to an architecture diagram this estate has.

MongoDB.what: The document database holding every WhatsApp conversation, on srv1340120.
MongoDB.why: Chat memory has no fixed shape and grows per turn, which suits documents. It is also the agent's memory: the reply depends on loading the prior messages back out.

GPT-5 mini.what: The OpenAI model Yamini generates replies with.
GPT-5 mini.why: Output tokens cost 8x input on this model, so reply length is the single biggest cost lever. At ₹0.59 per conversation it is a rounding error next to a ₹1,080 Google lead.

WhatsApp Cloud API.what: Meta's own WhatsApp API, used directly with no BSP in between.
WhatsApp Cloud API.why: Going direct means Meta's rate card is the real cost. A BSP would add 2x to 5x on top, turning a ₹1.04 marketing message into ₹2 to ₹5.

BSP.what: Business Solution Provider, a reseller that fronts the WhatsApp API.
BSP.why: KW does not use one. That is a deliberate saving and worth protecting.

Meta Cloud API.what: The inbound webhook and outbound send endpoint for WhatsApp.
Meta Cloud API.why: Every message in and out crosses it. It is the boundary between Meta's infrastructure and this estate.

service message.what: A WhatsApp reply sent inside the 24 hours after a customer messages you.
service message.why: Meta charges nothing for it. Yamini's replies are all service messages, so the conversational agent costs nothing on the WhatsApp line. Only outbound broadcasts are billed.

LangChain.what: The message format the chat history is stored in.
LangChain.why: It fixes the shape of each turn as type plus data, which is what lets the agent reload a conversation and continue it.

sessionId.what: The phone number in E.164 without the plus, used as the conversation key.
sessionId.why: One number is one conversation forever, so memory survives across days without any session concept.

leadAnalysed.what: A flag on a conversation record marking it as processed by the Qualification Agent.
leadAnalysed.why: Records without it are never queued. That single missing flag is why 504 of 27,368 conversations have a verdict.

IVR.what: The phone menu that hands callers off to WhatsApp.
IVR.why: A second inbound source alongside ads. It is 5.5% of leads, so worth keeping but not worth optimising.

Meta CAPI.what: Conversions API, the server-side way to report conversions back to Meta.
Meta CAPI.why: It closes the loop so Meta can optimise ad delivery on real outcomes rather than clicks. Currently inactive, which contradicts the architecture brief.

Enhanced Conversions.what: Google's equivalent of CAPI, sending hashed first-party data back to Google Ads.
Enhanced Conversions.why: Live and running daily, which is the reverse of what the architecture brief claims.

Customer Match.what: Uploading a customer list to Google to target or exclude those people.
Customer Match.why: Built, tested and deliberately parked while Meta was prioritised.

ufw.why: It is the only thing between a service bound to 0.0.0.0 and the internet. All three servers now have it active; two of them did not on 18 Aug.

certbot.what: The Let's Encrypt client that issues and renews TLS certificates.
certbot.why: Its inventory is the ground truth for which hostnames actually have a certificate. A hostname serving 443 that certbot has never heard of is a problem.

uvicorn.what: The ASGI server running the FastAPI dashboards.
uvicorn.why: Each dashboard is a uvicorn process on a loopback port with nginx in front. Knowing the port is how a hostname gets traced to the code behind it.

gunicorn.what: A pre-forking WSGI server, used for the Flask apps and one superseded FastAPI deployment.
gunicorn.why: fastapi_app.service is a gunicorn unit targeting the same port as the uvicorn one that replaced it, which is why it fails on every boot.

Traefik.why: It used to own 80 and 443 here. It no longer does: nginx took over, and both Traefik containers are now dead weight, one stuck in Created for 115 days and one in a restart loop.

cloudflared.what: Cloudflare Tunnel, an outbound connection that publishes a service without opening a port.
cloudflared.why: kwatch.leadq.co.in reaches its app this way, so it never passes through nginx. Changing nginx will not affect it, and debugging it by reading nginx config will not work.

MongoDB Atlas.what: MongoDB's hosted service, external to these servers.
MongoDB Atlas.why: Yamini ran on it until the April migration. LeadQ still reads from it, which is the unresolved split-brain: nobody has confirmed whether anything still writes there.

Batch API.why: The qualification backlog is not time-sensitive, so it applies cleanly. It is what turns a ₹3,112 backfill into ₹1,556.

prompt caching.what: Charging 90% less for input tokens that repeat between calls.
prompt caching.why: Yamini's system prompt is byte-identical on every turn, which is the textbook case. Turning it on is a 34% saving for no behavioural change.
